items.title: ASML says it's getting order interest through 2030 as profit smashes expectations
AI math isn't mathing: infrastructure spending forecast to outstrip expected revenue
Anthropic to disclose new revenue numbers as AI lab financials become central to tech trade
Failure of Australia’s Largest IPO in Decades Sends Tremors Through AI Trade
Bank of America Survey Shows Investors Are Split on AI Bubble Risks

entries.headline: ASML, the Dutch maker of the machines that print the most advanced chips, reported third-quarter profit above forecasts and said some customers are already asking about orders for 2029 and 2030.
entries.summary: Anadolu Agency reports that ASML, the Dutch company that is the world's only maker of extreme ultraviolet lithography machines (the tools chipmakers use to print advanced chips), earned €4.96 billion ($5.55 billion) in the third quarter, above analysts' expectations, although its sales of €11.66 billion were slightly below forecasts. Chief executive Christophe Fouquet said some customers are interested in orders for 2029 and even 2030, and ASML raised the lower end of its full-year sales forecast to between €44 billion and €45 billion.
entries.importance_line: Demand for the machines that make AI chips is running ahead of ASML's planned supply for 2027 and 2028, which could keep advanced chips tight for the companies, and eventually the people, who depend on AI services; this is the company's own outlook, and its quarterly sales were slightly below forecasts.
entries.notes: Original (CNBC, 403) and Reuters (401) blocked here; text read on Anadolu Agency, which reported the results itself without crediting another outlet. Score kept at 8.

entries.headline: Analyst firm Gartner forecasts that spending on AI data centres through 2030 will far exceed the revenue they can earn, putting many smaller AI computing providers at risk.
entries.summary: The Register reports that analyst firm Gartner estimates AI data centre operators would need about $8.5 trillion in revenue by 2030 to cover planned spending and earn a 12 percent return, but expects no more than $3.6 trillion. Gartner forecasts that 80 percent of neoclouds, companies that rent out AI computing power, will not survive as independent firms beyond 2030, while large cloud providers (hyperscalers) should cope better because their businesses reach beyond AI.
entries.importance_line: A forecast gap of trillions of dollars between AI building costs and AI revenue could mean write-downs, failed smaller providers and tighter funding, which would matter to investors, lenders and the companies that rent AI computing power; it is one analyst firm's projection, and Gartner's Will Sommer said not everyone is in trouble.
entries.notes: Full article read. Forecast figures are Gartner's, relayed by The Register; no independent check.

entries.headline: Anthropic is set to share its third-quarter financial figures with investors at a private meeting on 14 October, a step toward a possible stock market listing.
entries.summary: Reports from The News International and TradingKey, and a Wall Street Journal report relayed by Forbes Australia, say Anthropic will hold a closed-door investor day at its San Francisco headquarters on 14 October and disclose third-quarter financial data to institutional investors for the first time ahead of a possible initial public offering (IPO, a company's first sale of shares to the public). Media reports cited by TradingKey point to a target valuation of about $2 trillion and a possible November listing, but the offering size, valuation and date remain uncertain and Anthropic has not made its registration filing public.
entries.importance_line: The first detailed numbers from a leading AI developer could shift how investors judge AI company spending and profits, which matters to those who hold or may buy AI-linked shares; the figures were not yet public, and Anthropic has not confirmed the valuation or listing date reported by the media.
entries.notes: Desk-built entry (source AI News Desk) because CNBC's original is blocked (403) and no single read outlet credits it. CNBC original link: https://www.cnbc.com/2026/10/13/anthropic-q3-financials-ipo.html. Read page: TradingKey.

entries.headline: Australian data centre company Firmus has cancelled its planned stock market debut, and AI infrastructure companies elsewhere are now delaying or rethinking their own listings.
entries.summary: The Wall Street Journal reports, as relayed by Forbes Australia, that Firmus Grid, an Australian AI data centre company with close ties to Nvidia, cancelled what would have been the country's largest stock market debut in 30 years and now plans to raise money privately and list in the US next year, according to a person familiar with the matter. The cancellation dates from about 12 Oct 2026; the new element is that AirTrunk, another Blackstone-backed data centre operator, has pushed its Singapore listing back to the first half of next year, and the Journal says investors are becoming more selective about AI infrastructure companies.
entries.importance_line: If AI data centre builders cannot raise outside money easily, new AI computing capacity could arrive more slowly and smaller companies and their investors take the first losses; the report leans on bankers and an unnamed source, and it is not yet clear whether the listing window will reopen.
entries.notes: WSJ original (https://www.wsj.com/finance/firmus-ipo-ai-trade-f490c240) paywalled (401). Text read on Forbes Australia, which credits the WSJ; link is that page. Raise amount quoted as '$5 billion' without a currency. Stale-event rule applied (score 6 to 5).

entries.headline: A Bank of America survey found professional investors holding more technology stocks than at any time since 2020, while they are almost evenly split on whether AI shares are in a bubble.
entries.summary: Bloomberg reports, in a story carried by Yahoo Finance, that Bank of America's October fund manager survey found 37% of managers overweight technology stocks (holding more of them than a standard benchmark does), up from 30% a month earlier and the highest since August 2020. About 45% of respondents expect an AI bubble in 2027 while 42% do not, and global semiconductor stocks were named the market's most crowded trade.
entries.importance_line: Professionals with large sums are betting heavily on tech while nearly divided over a bubble, which can matter to anyone whose savings or pension sit in tech-heavy funds; it is a poll of 161 managers and an opinion, not a forecast.
entries.notes: Barron's original (403/401) not readable; Bloomberg text read on Yahoo Finance, which is the link. Survey of 161 participants, 2-8 Oct 2026.

entries.headline: ASML reported record quarterly profit and said chipmakers already want to book its machines for 2029 and 2030.
entries.summary: Chosunbiz reports that ASML, the Dutch company that is the sole supplier of the extreme ultraviolet lithography machines used to print advanced chips, posted third-quarter net income of 4.96 billion euros on sales of 11.66 billion euros, up 55 percent from a year earlier, and raised the low end of its 2026 sales forecast to 44 billion euros. Chief executive Christophe Fouquet said the planned supply for 2027 and 2028 will not fully meet demand and that some customers are "expressing an interest in placing orders with us for 2029 and even 2030", so ASML is studying a further capacity increase for 2028.
entries.importance_line: The company that builds the tools behind every advanced chip now expects demand to outrun its planned 2027 and 2028 capacity, which keeps the AI hardware build-out and the chip and power supply chains stretched, though sales fell slightly short of forecasts and demand could still cool.
entries.notes: CNBC pool link blocked (403); credited Chosunbiz, whose own report of the results was read, with AskTraders used for the analyst consensus and the CEO quote.

entries.headline: Gartner forecast that AI services will earn far less than the trillions being spent on AI data centres and that most specialist GPU cloud providers will not survive on their own past 2030.
entries.summary: The Register reports that research firm Gartner expects AI providers to spend nearly 1 trillion dollars on infrastructure in 2026 and a further 6 trillion dollars through 2030, while the AI revenue attributable to those data centres reaches no more than 3.6 trillion dollars against the roughly 8.5 trillion dollars needed to earn an acceptable return. Gartner predicts 80 percent of "neoclouds", companies that rent out graphics processors as a service, will be bought or will exit as independent businesses by 2030, with analyst Will Sommer telling the outlet that "not everyone is in trouble".
entries.importance_line: If the forecast holds, the companies renting out AI computing power and their lenders face write-downs that could reach several trillion dollars, which would slow the build-out that AI users and workers depend on, though Gartner's figures rest on its own assumptions and it says some providers will still do well.
entries.notes: Read directly. Gartner report date not given in the article.

entries.headline: Anthropic is showing its third-quarter revenue figures to a select group of investors for the first time as it prepares for a stock market listing.
entries.summary: CNBC first reported, as relayed by The News International and The Tech Buzz, that Anthropic, the maker of the Claude AI models, is presenting its third-quarter financials to potential investors at a meeting at its San Francisco headquarters on Wednesday, the first time it has opened its books in this way. The company has filed confidentially for a listing with the US Securities and Exchange Commission and, according to Reuters as cited by The News International, aims to list in November, though no date is confirmed and it is unclear whether the figures will include revenue earned through partners.
entries.importance_line: The figures will shape how investors value Anthropic and, by extension, the wider AI trade that has moved markets on rival revenue news, though it is not confirmed what the company will disclose or when it will list.
entries.notes: CNBC and Quartz blocked; text read on The News International and The Tech Buzz, which relay the report without a clear credit, so the chain is stated as CNBC first reported. Score lowered from 8 to 7: the disclosure had not happened when the reports ran and the original text was not read.

entries.headline: Australian AI data centre developer Firmus pulled what would have been the country's biggest share listing in decades after investors balked at a 44 billion Australian dollar valuation.
entries.summary: Forbes Australia reports that Firmus, a Nvidia-backed company that builds and runs AI data centres and was founded in Tasmania as a Bitcoin miner, withdrew its application to list on the Australian Securities Exchange on 9 Oct 2026 after too few investors took up shares offered at 11 Australian dollars, an offer meant to raise about 8 billion Australian dollars; the company says it will now seek private capital. Fund manager Jun Bei Liu of Ten Cap told the outlet that "confidence evaporated", and a piece by economist Marta Khomyn republished by Startup Daily notes that only two of Firmus's data centres are operating, that its valuation had risen almost eightfold in under a year, and that the Australian Financial Review has asked whether investor demand was misrepresented. The Wall Street Journal reported on 14 Oct that the failure is unsettling the wider AI trade.
entries.importance_line: Investors refused to pay for AI data centres that mostly exist on paper, a warning for other AI infrastructure floats and for the superannuation savers who would have bought in, though the pullback may be specific to Firmus's fast-rising valuation rather than the sector.
entries.notes: WSJ original blocked (401); its 14 Oct angle is known from the headline only. Score lowered from 6 to 5 because the underlying event is 9 Oct. Sources read: Forbes Australia (own reporting) and Startup Daily (The Conversation republication).

entries.headline: Bank of America's monthly survey found fund managers hold their biggest tech bet in six years even though nearly half of them expect an AI bubble next year.
entries.summary: The Wealth Advisor reports that Bank of America's October survey of 161 fund managers running 453 billion dollars found a net 37 percent overweight technology stocks, the highest reading since August 2020, while 45 percent expect an AI bubble to form in 2027 and 42 percent disagree. The survey names bets on global semiconductor stocks as the most crowded trade, puts cash at 3.9 percent of portfolios, below the level the bank treats as a sell signal, and ranks a disorderly rise in bond yields, with the 10-year US Treasury near 5.2 percent, as the biggest perceived threat, ahead of an AI bubble.
entries.importance_line: The professionals managing pension and savings money are crowded into chip and tech stocks while admitting the risk, which makes any change in AI spending or bond yields more likely to hit markets hard, though the survey measures opinions, not a forecast of when or whether a bubble bursts.
entries.notes: Barron's pool link blocked (401); The Wealth Advisor's own write-up of the BofA survey used and credited.

entries.headline: ASML, the sole maker of the most advanced chip-printing machines, says AI demand will outrun its supply through 2028 after a far bigger profit than expected.
entries.summary: AskTraders reports that ASML, the Dutch company that alone makes EUV (extreme ultraviolet) lithography machines used to print the most advanced chips, earned 4.96 billion euros in the third quarter, well above the roughly 4.1 billion analysts expected, while sales of 11.66 billion euros came in just under forecasts. Chief executive Christophe Fouquet said planned supply for 2027 and 2028 will not fully meet demand and that "some customers are expressing an interest in placing orders with us for 2029 and even 2030"; ASML set fourth-quarter sales at 14.2 to 15.2 billion euros and raised the bottom of its full-year range to 44 billion.
entries.importance_line: The company whose machines every leading chipmaker needs says it cannot build enough of them through 2028, which may keep advanced chips scarce and costly for device makers and AI companies, though the outlook rests on customers' own forecasts.
entries.notes: CNBC original blocked (403); also Reuters, Anadolu, Stock Titan and asml.com blocked. Facts from AskTraders, cross-checked with Startup Fortune.

entries.headline: Research firm Gartner forecasts that AI revenue will fall trillions of dollars short of the money being spent on AI data centres by 2030.
entries.summary: The Register reports that Gartner estimates AI data-centre operators would need about 8.5 trillion dollars of revenue by 2030 to earn a normal 12% return on nearly 7 trillion dollars of planned spending, but expects only about 3.6 trillion dollars of AI revenue in that period. Gartner predicts that 80% of "neoclouds", firms that rent out AI chips as a service, will not survive as independent companies beyond 2030, while the largest cloud providers should cope better because they earn money elsewhere.
entries.importance_line: If Gartner is right, investors and lenders face large write-downs and most small AI cloud providers would be bought or close, though this is one firm's model built on assumed returns.

entries.headline: Anthropic, the maker of the Claude AI assistant, is showing its third-quarter financial results to investors for the first time ahead of a planned stock market listing.
entries.summary: CNBC reports, as relayed by Stocktwits and The News International, that Anthropic will present its third-quarter financials to a group of institutional investors on Wednesday as it prepares an IPO that, by other reports, could value it near 2 trillion dollars; it has filed confidentially with US regulators, and Reuters reports a November listing that has not been confirmed. The figures matter beyond the company because AI lab revenue now moves chip and tech stocks: earlier this month, confusion over OpenAI's revenue figures shook the Nasdaq.
entries.importance_line: The first look at Anthropic's numbers will help investors judge whether AI lab revenue can support today's valuations and chip spending, affecting tech stock holders and pension funds, but the figures stay private for now and the listing date is unconfirmed.
entries.notes: CNBC original blocked (403); text read via Stocktwits on TradingView (https://www.tradingview.com/news/stocktwits:af9e8e8cf094b:0-anthropic-ipo-ai-lab-reportedly-to-share-q3-financials-with-investors-as-it-weighs-2-trillion-valuation/) and The News International. Writer is an Anthropic model; written neutrally from sources.

entries.headline: Australian AI data-centre builder Firmus scrapped what would have been the country's biggest stock market listing in decades after investors balked at its price.
entries.summary: Forbes Australia reports that Firmus, a Tasmania-based "neocloud" that builds AI data centres and rents out Nvidia chips, withdrew its ASX listing, announced about 12 Oct 2026, after too few funds bought shares offered at 11 Australian dollars to raise 8 billion at a 44 billion Australian dollar valuation. Its value had jumped from under 2 billion a year earlier on last year's revenue of 50 million; eToro analyst Josh Gilbert said investors would not pay up front "for capacity that's still largely on the drawing board".
entries.importance_line: Investors refused to pay 44 billion Australian dollars for AI data centres that are mostly still plans, a warning for other AI infrastructure listings and their backers, though Firmus says it will raise money privately and may list in New York instead.
entries.notes: WSJ original blocked (401 paywall); its market-tremors angle not read. Withdrawal date inferred from coverage timestamps (12 Oct 2026).

entries.headline: Professional investors hold more tech stocks than at any time since 2020, even though nearly half expect an AI bubble next year, a Bank of America survey finds.
entries.summary: The Wealth Advisor reports that Bank of America's October survey of 161 fund managers found a net 37% overweight technology, up from 30% in September and the highest since August 2020, while 45% expect an AI bubble in 2027 and 42% do not. Managers named chip stocks the market's most crowded trade and ranked a disorderly rise in bond yields as the biggest risk, ahead of an AI bubble, with 37% saying a 6% ten-year US Treasury yield would push them from stocks to bonds.
entries.importance_line: With big funds crowded into the same chip stocks, a change in mood or rising bond yields could trigger fast selling that reaches ordinary savers' pensions and index funds, though most managers still expect strong earnings.
entries.notes: Barron's original blocked (401 paywall). Facts cross-checked with CNBC-TV18.

entries.headline: Australian AI data-centre builder Firmus pulled its planned 44 billion Australian dollar share listing after weak investor demand.
entries.summary: The Wall Street Journal and Forbes Australia report that Firmus, a Nvidia-backed company that builds AI data centres and rents out computing power, withdrew what would have been Australia's largest stock market listing in decades after funds would not buy enough shares at its asking price. Forbes Australia notes Firmus earned 50 million Australian dollars in revenue last year while seeking a 44 billion dollar valuation, and rising bond yields added to doubts about the debt it needs to build.
entries.importance_line: Investors refused a high price for AI data centres that are mostly not yet built, which may make other AI listings harder, though Firmus says it will seek private money instead.
entries.notes: WSJ blocked (401); facts read from Forbes Australia's own reporting. Exact withdrawal date not stated in text read; it may fall slightly before 13 Oct.

entries.source: Bank of America survey, reported by The Wealth Advisor

Respondents named semiconductor stocks the most crowded trade and ranked a disorderly rise in bond yields as a bigger threat than an AI bubble.

entries.headline: ASML, the only maker of the machines that print the most advanced chips, posted a record quarter and said demand now outruns what it can build.
entries.summary: AFP reports that ASML, the Dutch company that alone makes the extreme ultraviolet (EUV) lithography machines needed for the most advanced chips, earned a net profit of 5.0 billion euros in the third quarter, up from 2.1 billion a year earlier, on record sales of 11.7 billion euros, and raised its 2026 sales forecast to 44 to 45 billion euros. Chief executive Christophe Fouquet said demand is outstripping supply, that ASML is looking to lift 2028 capacity beyond the 30 percent increase already planned, and that "some customers are expressing an interest in placing orders with us for 2029 and even 2030."
entries.importance_line: The Dutch firm says customers keep raising their AI-driven equipment plans and some already ask about orders for 2029 and 2030, which affects how fast chipmakers can add AI capacity and what that capacity costs; interest in future orders is not the same as booked orders.
entries.notes: CNBC original blocked (Access Denied). AFP text read as carried by The Economic Times; url is that page. Pool title's 'order interest through 2030' kept as interest, not orders.

entries.headline: Research firm Gartner forecasts that AI revenue will fall trillions of dollars short of paying for planned AI data center spending by 2030.
entries.summary: The Register reports that Gartner, the technology research firm, expects AI providers to spend nearly $1 trillion on AI infrastructure in 2026 and another $6 trillion from 2027 to 2030, while AI revenue tied to data centers over that time reaches no more than $3.6 trillion, far below the $8.5 trillion Gartner says operators would need to earn a 12 percent return on their investment. entries.notes: Full text read. Figures are Gartner forecasts.

entries.headline: Anthropic is showing its third-quarter financial results to a group of big investors for the first time as it prepares for a possible stock market listing.
entries.summary: CNBC reports, citing people familiar with the matter and as relayed by Stocktwits, that Anthropic, the maker of the Claude AI models, is sharing its third-quarter financials with a group of institutional investors on Wednesday, 14 Oct, ahead of an initial public offering that could reportedly value it at $2 trillion; Reuters has reported a November listing, which is not confirmed. The meeting matters because AI lab revenue now moves public markets: earlier this month, conflicting reports of OpenAI's annual revenue, $70 billion or about $50 billion, rattled chip stocks and the Nasdaq.

entries.notes: CNBC page blocked (Access Denied); CNBC's report read via Stocktwits, which credits it; url is CNBC's original. Figures are private to investors.

entries.headline: The collapse of Firmus's planned stock market listing, Australia's largest in decades, is still hurting the AI data center company's partners and testing investor appetite for AI building projects.
entries.summary: Firmus, an Nvidia-backed Australian developer of AI data centers, withdrew its share sale on 9 Oct 2026 after weak demand for an offer that would have valued it at A$44 billion, up from under A$2 billion a year earlier on revenue of A$50 million, Forbes Australia reports; the company says it will seek private money instead, and analysts quoted by Forbes Australia blame the high price and rising bond yields. Days later the damage is spreading: Proactive Investors reports that building partner Maas Group has lost 36 percent of its market value over A$1.1 billion of Firmus-linked contracts, and broker Jefferies cut its rating on Maas.
entries.importance_line: Investors refused to pay up front for AI data centers that are mostly still plans, which hit contractors and their shareholders first and may make it harder and dearer for similar projects to raise money; Firmus says it can fund itself privately, and its bigger backers remain confident.
entries.notes: WSJ original blocked (captcha); its 'tremors through AI trade' angle unread. Desk-built from Forbes Australia (13 Oct) and Proactive Investors (12 Oct); url is Forbes Australia. Proactive gives the raise as $5 billion (likely US dollars), Forbes Australia A$8 billion.

entries.importance_line: Chipmakers appear to be planning AI production capacity years ahead, which matters to anyone relying on AI services and to ASML's investors, but order interest is not a commitment and the figures are unconfirmed.
entries.notes: CNBC page blocked (HTTP 403); Stock Titan also 403. Details read at The Tech Buzz, which is a thin secondary write-up with no profit figures and no named ASML executive; no exact profit or order numbers could be verified. 'Order interest' is not booked orders. Score lowered 8 to 7 for unverified figures.

entries.headline: Research firm Gartner forecasts that AI companies will earn far less than they plan to spend on data centres and computing equipment by 2030.
entries.summary: The Register reports, citing Gartner, that AI providers are expected to spend nearly $1 trillion on AI infrastructure in 2026 and a further $6 trillion from 2027 to 2030, while related AI revenue is forecast at no more than $3.6 trillion against the $8.5 trillion Gartner says would be needed for a 12 percent return. Gartner expects about 80 percent of neoclouds, companies that rent out AI computing power, to disappear as independent businesses by 2030, with large cloud providers better placed.
entries.importance_line: If the forecast holds, AI-infrastructure investors and smaller computing providers face losses and mergers, which could slow how fast AI services expand for customers, but it is one firm's projection and Gartner itself says some companies will do well.
entries.notes: Full article read at The Register. This is an analyst forecast, not a result.

entries.headline: Anthropic, the maker of the Claude AI assistant, is reported to be sharing its third-quarter financial results with investors this week as it prepares for a possible stock market listing.
entries.summary: CNBC reports, citing people familiar with the matter and as relayed by Stocktwits, that Anthropic will show institutional investors its third-quarter financials on Wednesday 14 Oct 2026 while weighing an IPO (a first public share sale) at a valuation of up to $2 trillion. The company has confidentially filed with US regulators but has not made its filing public, Reuters' reported November listing date is unconfirmed, and a legal dispute over its US government supply-chain-risk label adds uncertainty.
entries.importance_line: Anthropic's numbers will show how much money AI products are actually earning, which matters to investors and to the AI companies that depend on them, but the figures are not yet public and the IPO timing is unconfirmed.
entries.notes: CNBC page (403) and Quartz and Benzinga blocked. Text read at TradingView (Stocktwits write-up of CNBC). Numbers not yet disclosed. Score lowered 8 to 7 because the figures are not out and rest on unnamed sources.

entries.headline: Firmus, an Australian builder of AI data centres, cancelled its planned stock market listing after investors did not buy enough shares.
entries.summary: Forbes Australia reports that Firmus, which builds data centres for AI companies and counts Nvidia as an investor, withdrew its application to list on the Australian stock exchange after investor interest fell short of the $8 billion it sought at a $44 billion value. The company says it will now look for private funding; the Wall Street Journal's headline says the failure rattled the wider AI trade, which we could not verify.
entries.importance_line: The collapse shows investors are less willing to pay very high prices for AI infrastructure companies, which affects Firmus's backers and Australian investors, though one failed deal does not prove a wider trend.
entries.notes: WSJ page blocked (HTTP 401). Read Forbes Australia's own reporting on the same story; the WSJ headline's 'tremors through AI trade' claim could not be verified. Currency read as Australian dollars from the article's own usage.

entries.headline: A Bank of America survey of fund managers found that more investors hold technology stocks than at any time since 2020, while nearly half expect an AI bubble by 2027.
entries.source: Latin Times, citing Bank of America
entries.summary: Latin Times reports that Bank of America's October fund manager survey found 37 percent of respondents overweight technology, up from 30 percent a month earlier and the highest since August 2020, while roughly 45 percent expect an AI bubble by 2027 and about 42 percent disagree. The split matters because big technology companies report earnings in late October, which investors see as a test of whether heavy AI spending is paying off.
entries.importance_line: Pension and fund investors are heavily exposed to AI stocks while unsure about a bubble, and a sharp fall could hit savings and company funding, but a survey measures opinion, not what will happen.
entries.notes: Barron's blocked (HTTP 401). Read Latin Times, which reports the BofA survey and adds its own commentary; BofA survey figures are as relayed, not checked against BofA's release.

entries.headline: Dutch chip-tool maker ASML says it cannot fully meet demand for its machines in 2027 or 2028.
entries.summary: Bloomberg reports, as relayed by The Next Web, that ASML, the only company that makes the machines for the most advanced chips, raised the low end of its 2026 sales forecast to 44 to 45 billion euros. The Next Web quotes CEO Christophe Fouquet saying, "Customers are asking every single day for more tools," which suggests how long chipmakers expect AI spending to last.
entries.importance_line: ASML raised the low end of its 2026 sales outlook and says some customers want machines for 2029 and 2030, so the chip build-out looks set to run for years, though this is stated customer interest rather than reported signed orders.
entries.notes: Original CNBC (pool link) blocked; read The Next Web, which credits Bloomberg only for the guidance raise. Quote and order interest attributed to The Next Web. The pool headline's profit-beat claim is not in the text read and is not stated. url is the page read (the original is not reachable).

entries.headline: Gartner says AI revenue will not profitably cover planned data-centre spending through 2030.
entries.summary: The Register reports, citing a Gartner research report, that AI providers are expected to spend nearly $1 trillion on infrastructure in 2026 and about $6 trillion more from 2027 to 2030. Gartner estimates that AI revenue attributable to data centres will reach no more than $3.6 trillion over that period, far short of the $8.5 trillion it says would be needed for a 12 percent return, which could force write-downs and a shake-out in which 80 percent of neocloud operators, the firms renting out AI computing power, stop being independent by 2030.
entries.importance_line: Gartner's new forecast says AI revenue falls short of planned AI data-centre spending through 2030, which would hit neocloud rental firms and their investors first, while Gartner expects the big cloud companies to cope better; the doubt is that this is one research firm's forecast, not a measured result.
entries.notes: Gartner report is a forecast; the summary keeps the hedges ('estimates', 'forecasts'). The Register is the reporter and the url is its page. Summary is two sentences, slightly long; shortening it is a Full Report editor's call.

entries.headline: Anthropic plans to share new financial figures with investors as it prepares a possible stock-market listing.
entries.summary: CNBC reports, citing people familiar with the matter, that Anthropic, the maker of the Claude AI models, plans to share its third-quarter financials with institutional investors on Wednesday, 14 October, as it prepares a possible initial public offering (its first sale of shares to the public) that could value it at about $2 trillion. The figures should show how fast revenue and profit are growing at a leading AI lab, which will help investors judge AI lab valuations, though no listing date has been confirmed.
entries.importance_line: Anthropic plans to show quarterly revenue and profit figures to investors, which affects investors weighing AI lab valuations and then the wider AI stock market; the doubt is that the figures are not yet public and no listing date has been confirmed.
entries.notes: CNBC original (the url) blocked for us (HTTP 403); facts read through Stocktwits' account of the CNBC report, which names CNBC as reporter. Score lowered 8 to 7: the numbers are not out and the disclosure is a plan. Reuters' November listing report is cited second-hand and not used in the summary.

entries.headline: Australian AI data-centre firm Firmus has withdrawn its plan to list on the Australian Securities Exchange.
entries.summary: Forbes Australia reports that Firmus has withdrawn its application to list on the Australian Securities Exchange after investors showed too little interest in its offer of A$8 billion of shares at a A$44 billion market value, and that it will now seek private capital. The listing was set to be the biggest in decades, and an eToro analyst said investors would not pay a high price up front for AI capacity that is still largely on the drawing board.
entries.importance_line: Australian investors who hoped for a local AI listing lose it for now, and the ASX loses its planned biggest IPO in decades; the doubt is that Firmus says its long-term prospects remain strong and will now rely on private capital, which is not yet secured.
entries.notes: Event before 13 Oct 2026, so stale for the news; score 6 lowered to 5. The WSJ original (pool link) blocked (401); its 'tremors' framing is not used. Forbes Australia's page date is 13 Oct 2026. Currency: the article uses $ for AUD and US$ for USD, so A$ is used. Subject to the NO OLD NEWS check (Part A step 9b).

entries.headline: A Bank of America survey finds fund managers split almost evenly on whether there will be an AI bubble in 2027.
entries.summary: Bloomberg reports, citing a Bank of America survey of 161 fund managers who oversee $453 billion, that 45 percent expect an AI bubble in 2027 and 42 percent do not. The share of managers overweight tech rose to 37 percent from 30 percent last month, the highest since August 2020, so many portfolios are heavily exposed to whether the AI rally holds.
entries.importance_line: The October survey shows tech overweight positions at their highest since 2020 while investors are split on an AI bubble, which affects fund managers and their clients first and then tech stocks; the doubt is that it is one bank's survey of 161 managers, not a market measure.
entries.notes: Barron's original (pool link) blocked (401). Yahoo Finance copy credits Bloomberg, so the source is Bloomberg under the copy-site rule; url is the Yahoo page read, since the Bloomberg link was not found. The phrase 'so many portfolios are heavily exposed to whether the AI rally holds' is our analysis of the overweight figure, not a reported fact; the Full Report editor may cut it.
